title: Basic Instrumentation for Water and Wastewater Operators
audience: Operators and trainees across the US and Canada preparing for certification exams and renewal in water and wastewater work.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic, a calculator and familiarity with treatment plants and pump stations. US customary units are primary with metric equivalents; all scenarios and facility data are fictional. Historian data, alarm records and SCADA record audits are covered in the applied instrumentation course.
introduction: Build the foundations of plant instrumentation: how an instrument loop works, the 4-20 mA signal and its live zero, how pressure, level and flow devices measure and mislead, what analyzers measure and how they drift, how basic control and alarms behave, and how to read trends and troubleshoot in a logical order. Each module ends with worked examples that name the usual mistakes. Safety content is recognition and purpose only, and facility procedures govern.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Measurement fundamentals
objectives: Describe the parts of an instrument loop and sort sensors into status, physical and analytical families.
Convert a 4-20 mA signal to engineering units and back, and explain the live zero.
Separate range, span, accuracy, resolution and repeatability, and explain calibration, verification, drift and uncertainty.
modules.lesson: ### Why operators need to understand the loop Every measured value on a plant screen has travelled through a chain of devices before it reached you. If you know the links in that chain, you can tell a process problem from an instrument problem, and that skill saves hours of chasing the wrong fault. > **Your job:** treat every reading as a measurement with a path behind it, and ask which link in the path could be wrong before you act on the number. A **sensor** is the part that responds to the process, by contact or, like radar, from a distance, and converts a process variable, such as pressure, level or pH, into a usable signal. A **transmitter** conditions that raw response into a standard signal and sends it to the controller and to the displays. The **controller** compares the signal with a setpoint, and a **control element** such as a valve, a blower or a variable speed pump acts on the process. The loop closes because the process changes, and the sensor sees the change. ### Three kinds of sensors Sensors fall into three families, grouped by what they report. The family hints at how the signal is usually used. - **Status sensors** report a condition: a valve is open or closed, a motor is running or stopped, a selector switch sits in AUTO or MANUAL. They drive alarms and interlocks, such as stopping a pump that has lost suction. - **Physical sensors** measure a physical property: flow, pressure, temperature, speed. Operators use them to judge equipment performance and to build trends. - **Analytical sensors** measure water quality: pH, chlorine residual, turbidity, ORP, dissolved oxygen, ammonia, nitrate, nitrite and sludge density. They often feed automatic control. For example, a dissolved oxygen reading is compared with a setpoint, and the difference decides how hard a blower works. **Worked example.** A fictional plant at Alder Fork has a selector switch on a lift pump, a pressure transmitter on its discharge and a dissolved oxygen probe in an aeration basin. The switch is a status sensor, the pressure transmitter is physical and the probe is analytical. If the pump does not start on an automatic call, the status sensor can show that the selector is in MANUAL, the physical sensor shows that discharge pressure did not rise, and neither tells you about oxygen. Each family answers a different question. ### Control elements and panel instruments A **control element** is the device that changes the process because a signal told it to: a modulating valve, an aeration blower or a variable speed pump. The sensor supplies the input and the element supplies the action. Without an element, a loop only reports; with one, it controls. Panel instruments are the operator's local window onto a process: meters and indicators, status lights, alarm annunciators, chart or digital recorders, pushbuttons and selector switches. An annunciator shows which alarm has tripped, a recorder keeps the history, and the pushbuttons and selectors let the operator command equipment. They are still part of the loop, so a lamp that stays lit or a meter that never moves deserves the same suspicion as a screen value. ### The 4-20 mA signal and the live zero Most transmitters send their reading as a current between 4 and 20 milliamps (mA). Current is used because the same current flows through the whole loop, so cable resistance does not change the reading as long as the loop has enough supply voltage, and current resists electrical noise better than a small voltage signal. The two ends of the signal match the two ends of the measuring range: 4 mA means the bottom of the range and 20 mA means the top. Why start at 4 and not 0? That is the **live zero**. A reading near 0 mA is a true electrical zero, which a healthy, powered transmitter does not send, so it points to a dead loop: a cut wire, a blown fuse, a dead power supply or a failed transmitter. If the range started at 0 mA, a real reading of zero and a dead loop would look the same. With a live zero, an empty tank (set as the bottom of the range) gives 4 mA and a broken wire gives about 0 mA, and the difference is obvious. Because the signal is a straight line, converting it needs only proportion. Use the **span** of the signal, which is 20 - 4 = 16 mA, and the span of the measurement. **Worked example 1: mA to engineering units.** A fictional flow transmitter on the Heron Bend main is set so that 4 mA = 0 gpm and 20 mA = 1,600 gpm (1 gpm = 0.0631 L/s). The loop reads 9.6 mA. **Step 1:** subtract the live zero: 9.6 - 4 = **5.6 mA** above zero. **Step 2:** divide by the signal span: 5.6 / 16 = **0.35**, or 35 percent of range. **Step 3:** multiply by the measurement span: 0.35 x 1,600 gpm = **560 gpm**. **Sense-check:** 9.6 mA is a little below the middle of the signal (12 mA), so the flow should be a little below half of 1,600. It is. **Worked example 2: engineering units to mA.** A fictional clearwell level transmitter spans 0 to 12 ft (1 ft = 0.305 m). The level is 3.0 ft. Fraction of range = 3.0 / 12 = 0.25. Current = 4 + 0.25 x 16 = **8.0 mA**. The two most common slips are skipping the 4 mA offset, which gives 0.25 x 16 = 4.0 mA, and using 20 instead of 16 as the span, which gives 4 + 0.25 x 20 = 9.0 mA. Both look plausible, so sense-check: a quarter of the range should sit a quarter of the way from 4 to 20 mA, which is 4 mA above the live zero. ### Range, span, accuracy, resolution and repeatability These terms are often mixed up, and exams like to test them. - **Range** is the lowest and highest value the instrument is set to measure, such as 0 to 1,600 gpm. **Span** is the difference between them, here 1,600 gpm. - **Accuracy** is how close the reading is to the true value. It is often quoted as a percent of span, so the same percent covers a bigger error on a bigger span. - **Resolution** is the smallest change the instrument can show. A display that steps by 0.01 has fine resolution, but fine resolution does not make a reading accurate. - **Repeatability** is how closely repeated readings agree when the same value is measured again under the same conditions. A meter can repeat well and still be wrong by a steady amount. **Worked example 3: error as a percent of span.** A fictional pressure transmitter spans 0 to 100 psi (1 psi = 6.89 kPa). A reference gauge shows 62.0 psi while the transmitter reads 63.5 psi. Error = 63.5 - 62.0 = 1.5 psi. Percent of span = 1.5 / 100 x 100 = **1.5 percent of span**. Whether that is acceptable is set by the manufacturer and your facility procedure, not by this course. ### Calibration, verification, drift and uncertainty **Verification** checks whether an instrument still agrees with a known reference, without changing it. **Calibration** compares the instrument with a reference and then adjusts it when it disagrees. Two adjustments appear in nearly every procedure: the **zero** adjustment sets the bottom of the range, and the **span** adjustment sets the top. A technician follows the manufacturer's method and the facility procedure for both. Instruments **drift**: the reading slowly moves away from the truth as a probe ages, a membrane fouls or electronics warm and cool. A zero shift moves every reading by the same amount. A span shift grows with the reading, so it hurts most near the top of the range. Verification is how drift is found before it matters. Finally, every reading has an **uncertainty**. The sensor, the transmitter, the conversion to a number and the sample itself each add a little. A reading of 560 gpm really means 560 gpm give or take an amount that depends on the instrument and the conditions, which is why a good operator trusts trends and cross-checks more than a single digit. Keep records of each calibration and verification, because a record of drift over months can show that an instrument needs repair before it fails outright.

### Fictional scenario: the Alder Fork clearwell

Alder Fork is a fictional plant. A level transmitter on its clearwell is set so that **4 mA = 0 ft and 20 mA = 12 ft**. This morning the loop current reads **13.6 mA**, the screen shows a level that looks high to the night operator, and a manual dip taken beside the tank gives **7.0 ft**.

### Your decision

Convert the current to a level, compare it with the dip, express the difference as a percent of span, and say whether you would call it a process change, drift or something else.
modules.assignment: Write a half-page note for the Alder Fork supervisor. Show the conversion step by step, give the difference as a percent of span, and say what you would do next. Do not state an acceptable error value; say the manufacturer and the facility procedure set it.
rubric: Converts 13.6 mA to 7.2 ft using (13.6 - 4) / 16 x 12 with units shown.
Gives the 0.2 ft difference as about 1.7 percent of span and treats it as a comparison to be judged against the facility's tolerance.
Names a sensible next step such as repeating the dip and recording the comparison, without quoting an accuracy limit.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Current to level: (13.6 - 4) / 16 = 0.60 of range, and 0.60 x 12 ft = 7.2 ft. The dip is 7.0 ft, so the difference is 0.2 ft, or 0.2 / 12 x 100 = 1.7 percent of span. Accept answers that call this a small difference to be compared with the facility tolerance, and that suggest a second dip and a log entry. Do not accept a learner quoting a required accuracy number as a rule; the manufacturer and the procedure set it. Drift is only suspected if the difference grows over repeated checks.

checks.prompt: In a basic instrument loop at a fictional plant, which device converts the sensor's response into a standard signal and sends it toward the controller and display?
choices: The control element, which acts on the process
The transmitter, which conditions and sends the signal
The annunciator, which lights an alarm window
The setpoint, which holds the target value
checks.explanation: The transmitter takes the sensor's raw response and turns it into a standard signal, usually 4-20 mA, for the controller and display. The "The control element, which acts on the process" choice moves the output side of the loop to the input side, since the element receives commands rather than sending the measurement. The "The annunciator, which lights an alarm window" choice names a panel indicator that only shows an alarm after the signal has already arrived. The "The setpoint, which holds the target value" choice confuses a number the operator enters with a device that carries the measurement.

checks.prompt: A fictional level transmitter is set so that 4 mA means 0 ft and 20 mA means 15 ft, and the response is linear. The loop reads 10.4 mA. The level is:
choices: 7.8 ft
9.0 ft
6.0 ft
checks.explanation: (10.4 - 4) / 16 = 0.40 of range, and 0.40 x 15 ft = 6.0 ft. The "7.8 ft" choice divided by 20 mA without removing the 4 mA live zero first. The "9.75 ft" choice divided by the 16 mA span but forgot to subtract the 4 mA offset from the reading. The "9.0 ft" choice turned the scale upside down, reading the level as the empty space above the water.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator asks why a 4-20 mA loop begins at 4 mA rather than 0 mA. The best answer is that the live zero:
choices: separates a true zero reading from a broken wire
lets the signal travel farther than a 0 mA start
doubles the resolution of the transmitter
reduces the cost of the cable run
checks.explanation: With a live zero, a real empty reading is 4 mA, while a dead loop sits near 0 mA, so the two cases look different. The "lets the signal travel farther than a 0 mA start" choice gives the wrong reason; current carries over long runs because it holds its value, not because of the starting point. The "doubles the resolution of the transmitter" choice mixes up the offset with resolution, which depends on the electronics and the display. The "reduces the cost of the cable run" choice has no basis, since the cable is the same whichever range the signal uses.

checks.prompt: A limit switch on a fictional valve reports open or closed. In the three sensor families, this is a:
choices: physical sensor, which tracks flow or pressure
analytical sensor, which measures water quality
status sensor, which can drive alarms and interlocks
control element, which acts on the process
checks.explanation: Open or closed, running or stopped, and AUTO or MANUAL are conditions, so they come from status sensors. The "physical sensor, which tracks flow or pressure" choice treats the valve as a measured physical quantity, but the switch only reports a condition. The "analytical sensor, which measures water quality" choice assigns it to the family for pH, residual and turbidity, which describe the water, not the valve. The "control element, which acts on the process" choice confuses a device that reports the valve position with the valve that moves.

checks.prompt: Which statement correctly separates calibration from verification?
choices: Calibration compares without adjusting; verification adjusts zero and span
Verification checks agreement with a reference; calibration also adjusts the instrument
They are the same task done at different intervals
Verification replaces the sensor; calibration cleans it
checks.explanation: Verification asks whether the instrument still agrees with a reference. Calibration compares and then adjusts zero and span when it does not. The "Calibration compares without adjusting; verification adjusts zero and span" choice reverses the two terms, since adjusting zero and span belongs to calibration. The "They are the same task done at different intervals" choice treats two different actions as one, ignoring that only one of them changes the instrument. The "Verification replaces the sensor; calibration cleans it" choice invents roles for each term that neither one has.

checks.prompt: A fictional pressure transmitter reads 2 psi above a reference gauge at every test point from the bottom to the top of its range. The pattern is best described as:
choices: a span shift, because the error grows with pressure
poor resolution, because the display steps are coarse
poor repeatability, because the readings scatter
a zero shift, because the error is the same size everywhere
checks.explanation: A constant error across the range moves every reading by the same amount, which is a zero shift. The "a span shift, because the error grows with pressure" choice describes an error that gets larger toward the top of the range, which is not what the test points show. The "poor resolution, because the display steps are coarse" choice mixes up a steady offset with the size of the smallest displayed step. The "poor repeatability, because the readings scatter" choice describes readings that disagree with each other, but here every test point has the same +2 psi error, a steady offset rather than scatter.

modules.title: Pressure, level and flow instruments
objectives: Compare pressure, level and flow devices and name what each measures and how.
Convert head to pressure and pressure to level, and use a rating to turn flume head into flow.
Explain why partly full pipes, air, fouling, foam and poor installation make instruments read wrongly.
modules.lesson: ### Pressure: why we measure it and how Pressure tells an operator whether a pump is working, whether a regulator is holding and whether a treatment step has the force it needs, such as a filter that is loading up or a membrane feed that is struggling. Two families of devices handle it. **Local gauges** usually use a Bourdon tube, C-shaped or coiled into a helix: pressure tries to straighten a curved tube that is sealed at its far end, and a linkage turns that small motion into a needle position. They need no power and show the value where you stand. **Transmitters** sense pressure with a diaphragm and send the result away, either as a pneumatic signal in older plants or as an electronic 4-20 mA signal, so a control room can see a pump discharge it never visits. A **differential pressure (DP)** device measures the difference between two points rather than one pressure against the atmosphere. DP across a filter shows loading. DP across a restriction in a pipe is also a way to measure flow, as discussed below. **Rate-of-flow control.** Pair a flow meter with an automatic control valve and a controller, and you can hold a flow steady. The meter reports the flow, the controller compares it with the setpoint, and the valve opens or closes to correct it. The valve is the control element and the meter is the sensor. ### Level: three ways to look at a tank Level information runs wet well pumps, tank fill and drain valves, and the level readings behind flume flow measurement. Methods fall into three groups. - **From above:** a ball float rides the surface and moves a switch or a transmitter arm. Ultrasonic and microwave (radar) sensors send a signal down and use the echo from the surface to find the distance. These two never touch the water. - **From below:** a pressure transmitter near the bottom senses the weight of the water above it. A bubbler tube releases a slow stream of air and measures the back pressure needed to push it out. A diaphragm bulb senses the pressure through a flexible membrane. - **Electrical:** conductance probes sense the water bridging two electrodes, and capacitance probes sense how the liquid changes an electrical field. They are common as high and low switches. Pressure from below converts to level because the pressure under a column of water depends on its depth, not on the tank's shape. One foot of fresh water makes 0.433 psi, and one psi is 2.31 ft of water (1 psi = 6.89 kPa; 1 ft = 0.305 m). **Worked example 1: head to psi.** A fictional wet well at Quill Run holds 8.0 ft of water above a submersible transmitter on the floor. Pressure = 8.0 ft x 0.433 psi per ft = **3.46 psi**. Check by the other constant: 8.0 / 2.31 = 3.46 psi. **Worked example 2: psi to level.** The same transmitter later reads 5.2 psi. Level = 5.2 psi x 2.31 ft per psi = **12.0 ft**. If the transmitter were mounted 1.0 ft above the floor, the true level would be 1.0 ft higher than the sensor reading suggests, which is why the mounting height must be part of the scaling. ### Open channel flow: flumes and weirs Most flow devices rest on one idea: flow equals area times average velocity. A meter either measures both, or measures one and relies on a known shape for the other. In an open channel, such as a plant influent channel or a sewer that is not running full, the water has a free surface with air above it. A **weir** (a notched dam) or a **flume** (a shaped, narrowing channel such as the Parshall flume) forces the water to behave in a known way. The device is the **primary element**: when it is installed correctly and flowing freely, its shape makes the depth of water, the **head** H, match the flow through a known relationship called the **rating**. The head must be read at the point the rating specifies, and a device flooded from downstream (submerged) no longer follows its free-flow rating. The **secondary device** is the level sensor, often ultrasonic, that measures that head. The sensor reports a level, and the rating converts it into flow. **Worked example 3: level to flow.** Use a *fictional* rating for practice: Q = 3.0 x H^1.5, with Q in cubic feet per second (cfs) and H in feet (1 cfs = 448.8 gpm; 1 cfs = 28.3 L/s). A real flume or weir uses its own published or manufacturer's rating. With H = 0.80 ft: **Step 1:** 0.80^1.5 = 0.80 x 0.8944 = **0.7155**. **Step 2:** Q = 3.0 x 0.7155 = **2.1465 cfs**, about 2.15 cfs. **Step 3:** convert: 2.1465 x 448.8 = **963 gpm**. Notice that flow rises faster than level: with a power above 1, the flow error in percent is about 1.5 times the level error in percent. The same level error in feet gives a bigger error in gpm at high flow, and at low head it is a bigger share of the reading. A level sensor that sits at the wrong distance from the flume, or a flume with debris on the floor, produces confident but false flow numbers. ### Closed pipe flow meters In a full pipe, four meter types are common. **Differential pressure meters** such as the venturi and the orifice plate narrow the flow so that pressure drops. The flow is proportional to the square root of the DP, so doubling the flow quadruples the DP. A transmitter (or the controller) applies a square root so the displayed flow is linear. **Worked example 4: square root.** A fictional DP flow transmitter has a maximum flow of 2,000 gpm at the top of its DP span. The DP reads 36 percent of span. Flow fraction = square root of 0.36 = 0.60. Flow = 0.60 x 2,000 = **1,200 gpm** (1 gpm = 0.0631 L/s). Do not read it as 36 percent of 2,000, which would be 720 gpm. This assumes the square root is not already applied in the transmitter. **Mechanical propeller meters** use a propeller in the stream whose speed tracks flow. Parts to recognise: the bearings the propeller turns on, a magnetic coupling that passes the motion through the wall without a leaking shaft, a totalizer that counts total volume, straightening vanes that calm the flow, and in some designs a cable drive. Worn bearings and debris can make them read low or stop. **Magnetic meters** pass water through a magnetic field and sense the small voltage the moving water generates between two electrodes. They have no moving parts and need a conductive liquid. **Transit-time ultrasonic meters** send sound pulses through the water and measure how flow changes their travel time, from outside the pipe in clamp-on designs. **Doppler** meters instead read the frequency shift off particles or bubbles in the water. **Worked example 5: area times velocity.** A fictional pipe with a 12 in (1 ft) inside diameter runs full at an average velocity of 3.0 ft/s. Area = 0.785 x 1.0 x 1.0 = 0.785 sq ft. Q = 0.785 x 3.0 = 2.355 cfs, and 2.355 x 448.8 = **1,057 gpm**. ### What makes each of them lie - **Partly full pipe.** A magnetic meter measures velocity and assumes the pipe is full, so a part-full pipe usually makes it over-read, because it applies the full-pipe area to a smaller flow area. Once the electrodes are uncovered the reading becomes erratic or meaningless, and many meters raise an empty-pipe alarm. - **Air bubbles and entrained gas.** Bubbles disturb magnetic, ultrasonic and pressure-based readings, and trapped air in liquid-filled impulse lines makes a DP signal offset, sluggish or unstable. - **Fouling and scale.** Coating on electrodes, ultrasonic faces and probes slows or distorts the signal. Grease and solids plug DP tubes. - **Foam and condensation.** An ultrasonic level sensor can echo off foam rather than water, and steam or heavy vapour changes sound speed. - **Wrong installation.** Too little straight pipe upstream of a meter, a sensor tilted off the surface, a transmitter mounted at a height the scaling does not know about, or an unlevelled weir produce errors that recalibrating the transmitter does not cure. A known mounting height can be put into the scaling; the others need the installation corrected. Many of these errors are steady. A steady error does not show up as noise, so it takes an independent check against a known value, such as a bucket test, a manual dip or a portable meter, or an inspection of the installation, to expose it. Record the cross-check in the maintenance log so the next operator does not repeat it. When a reading looks wrong, ask which of these conditions could apply before you suspect the electronics.

### Fictional scenario: the Quill Run lift station

Quill Run is a fictional lift station. A submersible transmitter on the wet well floor reads **4.6 psi**. The transmitter body is mounted **1.0 ft above the floor**. A small magnetic meter on the discharge reads high every dry morning, when the discharge pipe often runs part full.

### Your decision

Find the water depth above the floor, and say what the meter is doing wrong and what you would check or change.
modules.assignment: Write a short note for the station supervisor. Calculate the depth step by step with units, explain why the magnetic meter reads high in a part-full pipe, and name one installation fix. Do not quote any limit value.
rubric: Calculates 4.6 x 2.31 = 10.6 ft above the sensor and adds the 1.0 ft mounting height for 11.6 ft.
Explains that the meter assumes a full pipe, so a part-full pipe makes it over-read.
Suggests keeping the pipe full at the meter or relocating it, and cross-checking with an independent measurement.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Depth above the sensor is 4.6 psi x 2.31 ft per psi = 10.6 ft. Add the 1.0 ft mounting height for 11.6 ft above the floor. A magnetic meter measures velocity and assumes the pipe is full, so a part-full pipe makes it over-read, and uncovered electrodes make the reading erratic. Accept a fix that keeps the pipe full at the meter or moves it. Do not accept a span change as the fix; that hides an installation problem.

checks.prompt: In a fictional influent flume, the ultrasonic level sensor is the secondary device. Its job is to:
choices: measure the head so a rating can convert it to flow
measure velocity directly and multiply by pipe area
count the volume that has passed as a totalizer
shape the water so that depth tracks flow
checks.explanation: The flume is the primary element and the level sensor is the secondary device. The sensor reports head and the rating turns it into flow. The "measure velocity directly and multiply by pipe area" choice describes a closed pipe meter, not a flume, where the shape fixes the link between head and flow. The "count the volume that has passed as a totalizer" choice confuses a level sensor with the register of a flow meter. The "shape the water so that depth tracks flow" choice describes the flume itself, which is the primary element.

checks.prompt: A fictional wet well uses a bubbler tube. Compared with an ultrasonic sensor, the bubbler measures level from:
choices: above, by timing an echo from the surface
the side, by sensing water bridging two probes
below, by sensing the back pressure of the water column
above, by following the surface with a float
checks.explanation: A bubbler releases a slow stream of air, and the pressure needed to push it out tracks the depth, so it works from below. The "above, by timing an echo from the surface" choice describes the ultrasonic sensor that the question compares it with. The "the side, by sensing water bridging two probes" choice describes an electrical conductance probe, a third method. The "above, by following the surface with a float" choice describes a ball float, which rides the surface from above.

checks.prompt: A fictional wet well holds water 14.0 ft deep and a transmitter sits on the floor. Use 0.433 psi per ft of fresh water (1 psi = 6.89 kPa). The pressure at the transmitter is:
choices: 32.3 psi
6.1 psi
0.03 psi
14.4 psi
checks.explanation: Pressure = depth x 0.433 psi per ft = 14.0 x 0.433 = 6.1 psi. The "32.3 psi" choice multiplied by 2.31, which is the feet of water per psi and belongs on the other side. The "0.03 psi" choice divided the constant by the depth, inverting the relationship. The "14.4 psi" choice added the constant to the depth instead of multiplying.

checks.prompt: A fictional magnetic flow meter sits in a pipe that runs about half full. The meter will most likely read:
choices: low, because less water touches the pipe wall
true, because it senses velocity directly
true, because magnetic meters have no moving parts
high, because it assumes the pipe is full
checks.explanation: Flow is area times velocity. The meter applies the full-pipe area, so a half-full pipe usually makes it over-read, and uncovered electrodes can make the reading erratic or trigger an empty-pipe alarm. The "low, because less water touches the pipe wall" choice guesses that less water means a lower reading, but the meter multiplies velocity by the full area. The "true, because it senses velocity directly" choice forgets that flow needs area as well as velocity. The "true, because magnetic meters have no moving parts" choice mixes up reliability with correct use; a meter with no moving parts still needs a full pipe.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator wants a gauge that shows pressure at the pump discharge without any electrical or air supply. The best choice is:
choices: a Bourdon tube gauge
a 4-20 mA pressure transmitter
a differential pressure transmitter
a conductance level probe
checks.explanation: A Bourdon or helical gauge moves a needle mechanically as pressure tries to straighten a curved tube. The "a 4-20 mA pressure transmitter" choice needs loop power, so it cannot show a value without it. The "a differential pressure transmitter" choice also needs an electrical or air supply to work, which the operator wants to avoid. The "a conductance level probe" choice measures level with electrodes and not pressure.

checks.prompt: Flow through a venturi is proportional to the square root of the differential pressure. If a fictional operator doubles the flow, the differential pressure will:
choices: double along with the flow
rise by about 1.4 times
rise to about four times its earlier value
stay unchanged because the area is fixed
checks.explanation: If flow is proportional to the square root of DP, then DP is proportional to the square of flow, so doubling flow gives about four times the DP. The "double along with the flow" choice treats the relationship as a straight line instead of a square law. The "rise by about 1.4 times" choice applies the square root in the wrong direction. The "stay unchanged because the area is fixed" choice ignores that the flow through a fixed restriction depends on the pressure difference across it.

modules.title: Analytical instruments and basic control
objectives: Describe what pH, turbidity, conductivity, dissolved oxygen and chlorine residual analyzers measure and how each fouls or drifts.
Explain on/off, proportional and PID control and flow pacing with residual trim, including sample delay.
Describe setpoints, deviation alarms and why nuisance alarms are dangerous.
modules.lesson: ### What analyzers measure and how they go wrong Analyzers turn water quality into a signal, and many of them feed control loops. Each one has a measuring principle, a typical way of drifting and a need for a clean, representative sample. - **pH** uses a glass electrode that develops a small voltage depending on hydrogen ion activity. It is checked against buffer solutions of known pH. Coating, age and a dry or damaged bulb cause slow response and drift. - **Turbidity** shines light through the sample and measures the light scattered by particles. It is checked against reference standards. Bubbles read as particles, and a stained or scratched cell scatters stray light and usually reads high. - **Conductivity** measures how well the water carries current between electrodes, which tracks dissolved salts. Fouled contacting electrodes tend to read low, and the reading changes with temperature unless the instrument compensates. - **Dissolved oxygen (DO)** uses an electrochemical or optical sensing element. It is checked against air-saturated water or a lab method. Membranes foul, optical caps age, and too little flow past a membrane (electrochemical) sensor makes it read low. - **Chlorine residual** analyzers use a colour reaction or an electrochemical cell and are checked against a lab or portable test. Reagents run out, tubing grows slime, and the type of residual measured (free or total) must match what the permit asks for. Think of an analyzer as a small laboratory running without a chemist. It needs clean reagents or a clean sensing surface, a steady sample and regular comparison with a known reference. The operator's lab result at the same time and place is often the quickest reality check. When the analyzer and the lab disagree, do not assume which one is right: check the sample, the sensor, and the lab method. Other analyzers you will meet are ORP, solids, sludge blanket, ammonia and nitrate. They differ in principle but share the same questions: what is the sensor touching, how clean is it, and when was it last verified? **Sample conditioning** is everything done to bring a representative sample to the sensor: a tap in the right place, a short sample line, constant flow and, where the method allows, a strainer, cooler or degasser. Conditioning must not change what is measured: a strainer would remove the very particles a turbidity analyzer must see. A poor sample makes a perfect analyzer wrong. Calibration and verification of each analyzer follow the manufacturer's method and the facility procedure. ### Other physical sensors: temperature, weight and speed **Temperature** matters where heat controls a process, for example a chlorine evaporator and an anaerobic digester, whose microbes are sensitive to heat. Devices to recognise: liquid-in-glass thermometers, bimetal dials, thermocouples, filled expansion bulbs, thermistors, resistance temperature detectors (RTDs), infrared sensors and window tapes that change colour at set temperatures. **Weight** reveals chemical use directly. A **load cell**, a strain gauge arrangement that deforms slightly under load and sends a signal, is the usual way to weigh chlorine ton containers. The older weigh beam and the hydraulic load cell do the same job. The weight lost over a known time gives the average feed rate, provided nothing is leaking. **Worked example 1: feed from weight.** A fictional chlorine container on a scale falls from 1,852 lb to 1,780 lb over 8.0 hours (1 lb = 0.454 kg). Used = 72 lb. Rate = 72 / 8.0 = **9.0 lb per hour**, or 9.0 x 24 = **216 lb per day** at that rate. **Speed and proximity.** Speed sensors report back the speed of a variable speed pump or a metering pump using a tachometer generator, a non-contact frequency pickup, or an optical or magnetic counter. A proximity or zero-speed switch senses the presence or motion of a gear tooth, belt, valve stem or machine part. A broken belt on a dewatering press is a classic example: the zero-speed switch stops seeing motion and the interlock stops the press. ### Control concepts: on/off, proportional and PID **On/off control** switches a device fully on or off around a setpoint, like a home thermostat. It is simple and fine for sump pumps, but the process swings above and below the setpoint, and a gap called a deadband reduces rapid cycling. **Proportional control** changes the output in proportion to the error, which is setpoint minus measurement. The bigger the gap, the bigger the correction. A pure proportional loop usually settles slightly off the setpoint. **PID control** adds an **integral** action that keeps pushing while any error remains, so it removes that offset as long as the output has room to move, and a **derivative** action that responds to how fast the error is changing. Operators seldom tune PID, but should know that a controller hunting back and forth may be tuned too aggressively, may be fighting a sticky valve, or may be reacting to a bad signal. **Worked example 2: proportional output.** A fictional aeration basin has a DO setpoint of 2.0 mg/L, and the probe reads 1.4 mg/L. The controller has a 50 percent output with no error and adds 10 percent of output for every 1.0 mg/L of error. Error = 2.0 - 1.4 = 0.6 mg/L. Output = 50 + 10 x 0.6 = **56 percent** output, the blower speed command. ### Automatic loops in the plant **Chlorine residual loop.** Three signals work together. The flow meter gives **flow pacing**, so chlorine feed rises and falls with flow. The analyzer measures the residual downstream in the contact chamber and gives **residual trim**, a small correction to the pacing for changing demand. The setpoint controller combines them and moves the motorised chlorinator valve. A flow-paced, residual-trimmed feed system like this one therefore needs at minimum a flow sensor, a residual analyzer, a controller with a setpoint, and a motorised valve or feeder. The **sample location and transit time** matter. If the analyzer is far downstream, it only sees the result of a dose change after the water and the sample line have carried it there, and a loop that reacts to old information can swing. **Worked example 3: pacing and delay.** The fictional Linden Mill plant treats 1.5 MGD at a dose setpoint of 2.0 mg/L, with a feeder capacity of 100 lb/day. Feed = 2.0 x 1.5 x 8.34 = 25.0 lb/day, or **25.0 percent** of capacity. If the sample line holds 1.2 L and the sample flows at 0.40 L/min, the line adds 1.2 / 0.40 = **3.0 minutes** of delay before the analyzer even sees the water. **Digester temperature loop.** A temperature sensor in the digester feeds a setpoint controller, which positions a motorised valve on the heating water line. ### Pump control by pressure or by level Pumps are often started, stopped or speed-adjusted from a signal rather than by hand. A pressure control loop uses a pressure transmitter on the discharge main to hold a pressure setpoint; a service water or plant water pump is a common example, because its job is to keep the pressure steady for users. A level control loop uses a level sensor in a wet well or tank to start and stop pumps within a band; a lift station pump is the classic example. A return sludge pump drawing from a sludge well may also run on level, though many plants pace it to flow. Choosing the signal follows the job: pressure for steady delivery, level for holding a storage point. The instrument signal is only as good as its sensor and its setpoint, so a drifting level sensor can cycle a pump too often or let a wet well run dry. ### Setpoints and alarms A **setpoint** is the value you want. **Alarms** warn when the value leaves a sensible band: a **high alarm**, a **low alarm** and a **deviation alarm**, which trips when a measurement differs from the setpoint by more than a set amount, often catching a stuck control or a failed sensor sooner than a fixed limit would. **Worked example 4: a deviation alarm.** Suppose a fictional facility sets a deviation alarm at 0.5 mg/L on a DO loop with a 2.0 mg/L setpoint. At 1.4 mg/L the deviation is 0.6 mg/L, so the alarm trips even if 1.4 mg/L is still inside the fixed low and high alarm limits. That is the value of a deviation alarm: it flags a loop that is not holding its setpoint, perhaps because a blower tripped or the probe is fouled. Alarm values come from the operating permit, the design and facility procedure, not from this course. Their quality matters more than their number. **Nuisance alarms** that trip constantly teach people to acknowledge without reading, and the one real alarm gets lost among them. That is dangerous. Fix a nuisance alarm by finding the cause, such as noise, a poor setpoint or a fouled sensor, and record the change, rather than silencing it.

Calculates 1.2 / 0.40 = 3.0 minutes of sample line delay.
